Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read each wording and find the qualifier. Which case has the word that changes the figure the question expects?
Yes. The paper expects the 4 mL key, while current practice starts near 2 mL per kg per %TBSA and titrates to urine output.

Two first-day plans side by side. Plan X: crystalloid plus colloid per kg per %TBSA, with dextrose in water.
Plan Y: crystalloid alone, with no colloid on day one.
Which plan is the classic Parkland?

choices.label: Plan Y: crystalloid alone, with no colloid on day one
Plan X: the colloid plan, with dextrose in water
Both, since Parkland also has a colloid version
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Find the one ingredient that separates the plans: is colloid present on the first day? Then ask which formula the classic one is.
Yes. Parkland uses crystalloid alone in its first 24 hours; the colloid plan belongs to Evans and Brooke.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because plan X looks complete, with fluid, colloid and dextrose, like a textbook recipe. But that recipe belongs to Evans, which includes colloid, and the question asks about Parkland.

say.text: Parkland gives crystalloid alone in its first 24 hours; colloid is added later, once the capillary leak settles, about 8 to 24 hours.
Evans and Brooke carry colloid in their recipes, so plan X is their pattern, and the two plans differ on colloid.
Brooke, side by side with Evans. Brooke: 1.5 mL crystalloid and 0.5 mL colloid per kg per %TBSA, plus dextrose in water.
Evans: 1 mL crystalloid and 1 mL colloid per kg per %TBSA, plus dextrose in water.

choices.label: Evans carries twice Brooke's colloid per kg per %TBSA
Only the dextrose differs; the colloid is the same in both
Brooke is the Parkland recipe with colloid added from hour one
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Compare the colloid figure in each recipe, not just whether each recipe contains colloid.
Yes. Both carry colloid, but Evans gives a full mL per kg per %TBSA against Brooke's half a mL.
That is not the right choice.

It is tempting because Brooke and Parkland both start from a crystalloid base, so Brooke looks like Parkland with colloid added. But Brooke is its own recipe with its own colloid figure, not Parkland with a top-up.
Brooke: 1.5 mL crystalloid and 0.5 mL colloid per kg per %TBSA, plus dextrose in water.
Evans: 1 mL crystalloid and 1 mL colloid per kg per %TBSA, plus dextrose in water, so its colloid is twice Brooke's.
Patient A has burned ear cartilage. Patient B has a broad scald across the trunk and thighs, with no cartilage involved.
Which agent fits A and which fits B?

choices.label: A: silver nitrate; B: silver sulfadiazine
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which agent goes into eschar and cartilage, and which is the broad, painless default for a large area.
Yes. Mafenide penetrates eschar, so it suits ear cartilage; silver sulfadiazine is the broad, painless default for a large area.
That is not the right choice.

It is tempting because silver sulfadiazine is the agent most people reach for first, so it feels right for any burn. But the broad default is not the agent that penetrates eschar, and the ear needs penetration.

Patient A had a major scald, and endoscopy now shows an acute ulcer of the stomach.
Patient B has an old forearm burn scar that has become a non-healing ulcer with raised, everted edges.
Which ulcer is A and which is B?

choices.label: A is Curling's; B is Marjolin's
A is Marjolin's; B is Curling's
Both are Curling's, since both follow a burn
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at where each ulcer sits: the gut for one, and the skin of an old scar for the other. Which is which?
Yes. Curling's is the acute gut ulcer after major burns; Marjolin's is the squamous cell carcinoma that arises in a chronic scar.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both names come from burns, so the two are easy to swap. But check each patient's site: the gut and the scar are the two places these names are tied to.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both ulcers follow a burn, so one burn ulcer name seems enough. But the two differ in site and in what they become: an acute gut ulcer, and a cancer in a chronic scar.
Curling's ulcer is an acute stress ulcer of the stomach and duodenum after major burns, prevented with stress ulcer prophylaxis.
Marjolin's ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic burn scar.
Limb A: a circumferential full-thickness forearm burn; the fingers are now pale and the distal pulses are falling.
Limb B: a circumferential deep partial-thickness forearm burn; it is blistered, and the pulses are full.
Which limb needs an escharotomy now?

choices.label: Limb A only, with the pulses falling
Limb B, since deep burns form the eschar
Both, since any circumferential burn is cut
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what separates the limbs: depth, the circumference, and whether anything below the burn is losing its blood supply.
Yes. A circumferential full-thickness burn with falling distal pulses is the indication for release.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because deep burns look the most severe, so the word deep sounds like a reason to cut. But depth alone does not decide it: the burn must be full thickness and must compromise the limb.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because a ring of burn looks dangerous at any depth. But the circumferential qualifier is only part of it; the full-thickness qualifier and the falling pulses are what the cut treats.
Escharotomy is for circumferential full-thickness limb burns with distal ischaemia, cut through the eschar only.
The incisions run along the midlateral and midaxial lines; limb B has the depth but not the compromise.
Chest A: a full-thickness circumferential chest burn; the chest wall does not expand and the breathing is shallow.
Chest B: a superficial partial-thickness burn over the front of the chest; the breathing is normal.
Which chest needs an escharotomy?

choices.label: Chest A only, where breathing is restricted
Chest B, since a whole-chest burn is always cut
Both, since any chest burn restricts breathing
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which chest has both qualifiers: full thickness, and a restriction that is happening now.
Yes. A circumferential full-thickness chest burn that restricts ventilation is the chest indication.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because a whole-chest burn sounds serious, so it seems to need the cut. But size does not make the indication; the depth and the restriction decide it.
That is not the right choice.

It is tempting because the chest is a closed ring, so any burn there feels like a restriction. But only a full-thickness circumferential burn that restricts breathing is cut; a superficial one does not qualify.
The chest indication is a circumferential full-thickness burn that restricts ventilation.
Chest B is superficial partial-thickness with normal breathing, so it does not qualify.
Case A: hydrofluoric acid splashed on the hand while cleaning a tank.
Case B: a fire victim with carbon monoxide poisoning, confirmed on the blood test.
Which antidote goes to A, and which to B?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which case is an acid and which is a gas. Then match each antidote to its own poison.
Yes. Hydrofluoric acid burns get calcium gluconate, and carbon monoxide gets 100% oxygen.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both patients come from the same fire room, so their treatments feel interchangeable. But each antidote belongs to its own poison, and an acid splash is not treated like a gas.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because hydroxocobalamin is the antidote you learned for smoke, so it feels like the answer for case A. But it treats cyanide, a different poison, so it does not match a hand splash.
Hydrofluoric acid burns are treated with calcium gluconate.
Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with 100% oxygen, and cyanide with hydroxocobalamin: each poison has its own antidote.
